title: Stillness and Movement Are Not Two
reflection: Once or twice today, in the middle of what you are doing, take one slow breath. Feel the movement in, the stillness at the top, the movement out, the stillness at the bottom. Then notice that there is no line between them.

questions.q: Sarah says peace is the holiday she does not get, and real life is the noise to survive. What misunderstanding does Swamiji name?
o: That you must turn away from the moving world to reach quiet, so life and stillness seem enemies.
That you must work harder at your life to earn the peace, so rest is a prize for effort done.
That you must avoid all noise in the house to find the quiet, so a peaceful home is the key.
That you must give up the holiday altogether, so peace is a thing that belongs to other people.
questions.e: Stillness feels like an escape from life and life like an obstacle to stillness, so most people live in a tug-of-war. Swamiji says wherever there is real life, stillness and movement are both there at once, so Sarah is not failing at peace because her life is busy.
questions.c: The tug-of-war rests on a misunderstanding

questions.q: Kai notices he is still breathing and his heart is beating when he rests deeply; James notices something steady in him even in classroom chaos. What do the two observations show together?
o: Both are present: without movement, lifelessness; without stillness, agitation with no anchor.
Where there is life only movement is present, so stillness is something that appears only after death.
Where there is life only stillness is present, so movement is a surface appearance that can be ignored.
Where there is life the two take turns, so a person is either still or moving but never both at once.
questions.e: Pure stillness, total cessation, is not peace: a body with no movement at all is dead. The steady me under the chaos is Kai’s quiet bit aware of the mess. They are not fighting; they need each other.
questions.c: Both are present wherever there is life

questions.q: Swamiji asks the group to take one slow breath and find where the stillness ends and the movement begins. What does Kai find?
o: There is no line: it flows as one event, and stillness and movement are qualities of one whole.
There is a clear line at the top of the breath, so stillness and movement are two separate stages.
There is a line at the bottom of the breath only, so the breath is mostly movement with one pause.
There is nothing to find, since a breath is simply movement and stillness is a mental idea.
questions.e: Breathing in is movement, the pause at the top stillness, breathing out movement, the pause at the bottom stillness. Kai finds no actual line: it is one thing.
questions.c: In one breath there is no line

questions.q: In the picture of the ocean and its waves, what is a wave?
o: Not a little object crossing the water but the ocean itself, moving: a shape the ocean briefly takes.
A separate object travelling over the sea, which is carried along by the ocean beneath it.
A thing that takes something from the ocean when it rises and gives it back when it falls.
A disturbance that spoils the ocean, so that a perfectly motionless sea would be the healthiest.
questions.e: When the wave rises the ocean does not become less. Stillness is what the ocean is; waving is what it does. A perfectly motionless ocean would be ice, not water.
questions.c: A wave is the ocean moving

questions.q: A student says the two traditions in the lesson contradict each other. How does Swamiji describe them?
o: Two people on one shore: Advaita Vedanta describes the ground, Brahman and Śakti; Trika the pulse, Spanda.
Two people on different shores: Advaita Vedanta says only movement is real, and Trika says only stillness is.
Two stages of one path: a person studies Trika first and then leaves it behind to take up Advaita Vedanta.
Two opinions of equal weight: a person should choose the one that suits them best and ignore the other one.
questions.e: Swamiji says neither is wrong; both dissolve the same false split and arrive at presence in action: awareness that is steady and alive together. He links Spanda to the Vimarśa of the previous lesson. He also quotes Sri Ramakrishna: the still Reality and its active power are like fire and the fire’s power to burn.

questions.q: “Stability in the body is achieved by going still: if the constant adjusting stopped, the body would hold its balance even better.”
questions.e: The body holds steady temperature, blood chemistry and heartbeat through thousands of small corrections, which is called homeostasis. Stop the adjusting and the stable state collapses within seconds. The stillness of health is ceaseless dynamic activity held in balance.

questions.q: Sarah feels guilty for resting and has been near burnout. What does Swamiji say burnout is?
o: Movement with no felt ground: the recovery tide was suppressed, and rest is the tide that makes the next wave.
Working too hard for too long, so the cure is to give up work and to rest for as many weeks as it takes her.
A failure of will, so the cure is a firmer resolve to carry on until the tiredness finally goes away for her.
A fault of the body’s chemistry only, so the cure lies outside the mind and no change of outlook can help her.
questions.e: A person in burnout has not been working too hard; they have been refusing the ground that work draws its life from. Stress hormones surge in long waves instead of clean pulses, and sleep, mood and memory suffer. Rest is not laziness.
questions.c: Burnout is movement with no felt ground

questions.q: Kai reaches for his phone whenever it is quiet, because quiet feels as if something is wrong. How does the lesson read this?
o: Stillness has become unfamiliar, so silence feels like a gap to fill; the capacity to rest, viśrānti, can return.
He has too much energy, so the cure is more activity until the restlessness has been used up by him.
He has a weak will, so the cure is stricter rules for the phone and a firmer sense of self-discipline.
He has no ground at all, so the cure is to find a quiet place where he can stay for a long time and rest.
questions.e: Restlessness usually is not too much energy but the loss of a felt relationship with the ground. Viśrānti, restful presence, is a basic human need. The cure is not more movement but recovering the capacity to simply be here without doing. Kai’s practice: pause sixty seconds, watch the restlessness, and see whether the quiet is empty or just unfamiliar.

questions.q: A man says “it is all one, so my duties and relationships do not matter.” What does Swamiji say about this?
o: Ground without life: the ego borrowing a true idea as a hiding place; real practice deepens engagement.
It is the goal of practice, since the further a person can detach the deeper their understanding becomes.
It is the cure for anxiety, since a person who cares about nothing has nothing left to worry about at all.
It is a harmless view, since a person’s duties will look after themselves once the mind has found its rest.
questions.e: Burnout is life without ground; this is ground without life. The ground is not a hiding place from your life but the floor you stand on to meet it more fully. The real test of depth is how clearly and kindly you can engage.
questions.c: Ground without life is a hiding place

questions.q: “Anxiety, in this lens, is the wave convinced it is only surface, with no ocean under it, and it is not weakness but what happens when the ground is lost.”
questions.e: The anxious mind scans for threats and plans endlessly because it has nowhere that feels safe to rest. Practices that gently restore the felt ground, such as breath, the body and open attention, help so directly because they reconnect the moving mind to the steadiness that was always there.
questions.c: Anxiety is identification with the wave
